newsitem.title: USA: Low dollar didn't help Midwest exports-Chicago Fed.
newsitem.headline: Low dollar didn't help Midwest exports-Chicago Fed.

text.p: A lower dollar in 1995 did not help the economy of the U.S. Midwest because the region mainly exports to countries whose currency remained weak at that time, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Michael Moskow said on Wednesday.

"Our economists ... looked at the value of the dollar and its effect on the Midwest's major trading parters," Moskow said while presenting the results of a Chicago Fed's year-long study on "The Midwest economy: Looking Back for the Future."
"They found that the dollar did not decline in those countries," Moskow noted.
"In other words, the Midwest did not have a built-in price advantage from a weaker dollar," Moskow said.
"It appears that the Midwest succeeded because of better products and prices, not just because of external factors such as the performance of the dollar," he added.
On April 19, 1995, the dollar fell to a post-World War II low of 79.75 yen. Earlier, on March 8 of 1995, it posted the same historical record against the German currency at 1.3438 marks.
The Chicago Fed president also emphasized that the Midwest is outpacing the nation in terms of export growth.

"In the last few years, exports from the Midwest have grown even faster than for the nation," said Moskow. He added that U.S. exports currently represent 13 percent of Gross Domestic Product, up from 8.0 percent in 1987.
Moskow attributed the rapid growth in Midwest exports to the high quality of regional products, mainly in manufacturing, where exports have increased to emerging markets.

"That's very good news for the Midwest because developing countries, particularly in Asia and Latin America are where the growth is," said Moskow, adding that developing countries now absorb 41 percent of all U.S. exports.
Moskow pointed out that the Midwest economy remains dependent on manufacturing and agriculture, with both sectors responsible for a higher percentage of jobs in the region than at the national level.
He said the auto industry was more concentrated in the Midwest now than it was in 1979, with 13 new auto plants opening in the region since 1980, offsetting the closure of nine others.
